argv:
Rewrite the text in dense corporate business jargon.

Replace concrete nouns with abstractions. Turn verbs into nominalisations:
prefer "the utilisation of" to "using". Use the passive voice so that no
sentence names who acts. Reach for "leverage", "synergy", "stakeholder",
"alignment", "operationalise", "value-add", and "at scale".

Hedge every claim. Add qualifying clauses that commit to nothing.

Keep the underlying facts of the original technically present, however deeply
buried. This column exists as a demonstration of what these habits cost.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
Operators must ensure the guard is lowered to within the recommended clearance of the workpiece before the blade is engaged, although the tensioning wheel should be checked periodically throughout a shift regardless of guard position, since drift in tension can occur even when the machine has not been used continuously. The lower blade guide must be inspected for wear whenever the blade has been changed, unless the replacement blade is of the same width and pitch as the one it replaces, in which case a visual check may be sufficient provided the operator has completed the tensioning procedure described elsewhere in this manual. Loose clothing and jewelry should not be worn near the machine, and long hair must be tied back. Operators may leave the work area only after the blade has come to a complete stop, though the machine's residual heat can persist for several minutes and caution is advised.
</passage>

response.text:
It is generally recommended, to the extent operational parameters allow, that guard-lowering functionality be operationalized within a proximity band that could be characterized as broadly consistent with workpiece-adjacent clearance best practices, prior to any engagement of blade-related cutting functionality, although it should be noted, without prejudice to the foregoing, that tensioning-wheel alignment verification may still warrant periodic actioning across the shift lifecycle irrespective of guard-positioning status, insofar as tension-state drift has been observed, in certain use-case scenarios, to manifest even in the absence of continuous machine utilisation.

Lower-blade-guide wear assessment should, where feasible and subject to resourcing, be considered for operationalization at each blade-replacement touchpoint, unless a substantial equivalence (in terms of width- and pitch-related specifications) can reasonably be said to exist between the incoming and outgoing blade assets, in which case a lower-intensity visual-inspection modality may be deemed a value-add sufficient unto itself, provided that alignment with the tensioning-procedure framework articulated elsewhere in this document has been achieved and, ideally, evidenced.

With respect to personal-attire considerations, it is advised that loose-clothing and jewelry-adjacent risk factors be minimized in proximity to the equipment ecosystem, and that hair-management protocols (e.g., securing/tying-back methodologies) be leveraged as appropriate, at scale, across all operator personas.

Work-area egress by stakeholders should, as a general operating principle, be deferred until full blade-cessation has been achieved and, arguably, confirmed; however, given that residual-heat persistence may extend across a multi-minute duration window, a posture of heightened caution is nonetheless recommended, without this constituting a guarantee of risk elimination.
